turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Naidoo, shame, you look worn out. Come sit. Your daughter phoned the rooms quite worked up, so tell me, what's been happening at home?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, I'm tired, and I'm tired of the fuss. I didn't fall. I slid down, twice, and she turns it into a whole story.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. Tell me those two times, how they actually felt to you.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Tuesday I got up off the toilet, the room went funny, and I slid onto the mat. Yesterday in the passage, same thing, I went down slow. Nothing was sore and I got myself up.

[SEG0005] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, her daughter caught me at the desk. She says she found her mum on the floor both times, and yesterday she couldn't get up for about ten minutes. She called it a proper fall.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten minutes? Rubbish. She wasn't even there on Tuesday, and yesterday I was up before she came through. I slid, that's the end of it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you both. Apart from going down, how has the dizziness been for you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): When I stand up. It spins for a few seconds and I have to grab the wall. If I sit still I'm all right, it's just irritating.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, don't pin me down. A while, maybe a couple of weeks. I can't remember when it started.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And with the spinning, do you get a headache as well?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when it happens?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My chest is fine.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you short of breath? Or did you black out, properly lose consciousness?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No breathlessness. And I didn't black out, I knew where I was.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking these days, the blood pressure ones and anything you use for sleep?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Amloc in the morning, the five... no, the chemist changed it, it's the ten. Coversyl eight milligrams, also in the morning. And Stilnox at night, otherwise I'm awake half the night.

[SEG0019] person_3 (NURSE): There's a water tablet in the packet as well, Doctor. Hydrochlorothiazide twelve point five milligrams, one in the morning. The boxes match the Amloc ten and the Coversyl eight, and the Stilnox is ten milligrams at night.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the little water one. I take that too. I always forget the name.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): And you're getting all of them in every day?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the mornings I don't miss. The Stilnox, mm, most nights.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stilnox can make older people unsteady in the night. I think we should stop it, hey.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop it? Then I won't sleep at all. I'm already exhausted, don't take my sleeping tablet away.

[SEG0025] person_3 (NURSE): I did a lying and standing pressure before you came in. Lying was one fifty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-two. After a minute standing it was one twenty-two over seventy, pulse eighty-eight.

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Oh, that's a decent drop. I'm changing my mind, we'll leave the Stilnox alone. I'd rather you stop the morning water tablet, hydrochlorothiazide twelve point five milligrams, from today.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop the water one. Fine, as long as I keep the sleeping tablet. Will the dizziness actually go?

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is your blood pressure is falling when you stand, and the water tablet won't be helping that. It's not proved beyond that, but the numbers fit the spinning and the sliding.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen a moment. Heart sounds are regular, I don't hear a murmur. Your tongue looks a bit dry, though.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't drink much water. It sends me to the toilet and then the whole business starts again.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I get why you avoid it. Still, sip through the day, and when you get up, sit on the edge of the bed or the toilet, count to twenty, then stand and hold the wall.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Count to twenty. Ja, fine. I'm not a child, but I'll try. And those magazines out there are from about 2014.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the hip or the head from yesterday? I should have asked that sooner.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I told you already, nothing's sore.
[SEG0035] person_3 (NURSE): She was a bit unsteady walking in, Doctor, I watched her in the passage. I couldn't see a bruise on the arms.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Sister. I was going to skip bloods today... wait, no, with the water tablet and the Coversyl I do want urea and electrolytes. We'll get that done before you go.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): More needles. Wonderful. Can my girl take me home after? I'm done with today.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): She can take you. I want to see you back in two weeks, to recheck the standing pressure off that water tablet.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If I must.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you go down again or the dizziness gets worse, don't wait the two weeks, come straight back. And if you can't get yourself up, go to the emergency unit.
[SEG0041] person_3 (NURSE): I'll book the two weeks at the desk and draw those bloods now now.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

omissions.text: Orthostatic vital signs timing was specified: standing blood pressure/pulse were measured after 1 minute standing (122/70, pulse 88).
Headache was asked about and the answer was equivocal/uncertain ('Sometimes, not really'), not recorded.

There was an initial plan to stop Stilnox because it can make older people unsteady at night, but after seeing the orthostatic blood pressure drop the doctor reversed this decision and decided to leave Stilnox unchanged.
Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg was to be stopped from today.
Patient reported adherence detail: she does not miss the morning tablets, and takes Stilnox only most nights.
Patient specifically denied any soreness after the two episodes ('Nothing was sore') before later denying hip or head pain.
The patient said she did not fall but 'slid down' twice, got herself up, and yesterday was up before her daughter came through; this wording dispute is stronger than just 'ending up on the floor'.
